title: Infective Bone Disease
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Infective Bone Disease
headings.content: Infective bone disease, clinically recognized as **osteomyelitis**, is an inflammatory condition of bone and its structures caused by pyogenic organisms. While bone is normally resistant to bacterial colonization, introduction via trauma, contiguous spread from adjacent soft tissue, or hematogenous seeding can overcome local defense mechanisms. The infection triggers a destructive inflammatory cascade within the rigid confines of the bone cortex, leading to increased intraosseous pressure, microvascular thrombosis, and subsequent bone necrosis. In resource-constrained settings across Nigeria, delayed presentation of acute osteomyelitis often allows progression into chronicity, making early identification essential for preserving structural integrity and limb function.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Underlying Mechanisms
headings.content: When microorganisms invade bone tissue, the host inflammatory response initiates hyperemia, edema, and leukocyte infiltration. As pus accumulates within the medullary cavity, it tracks through Haversian canals to reach the subperiosteal space, stripping the periosteum of its blood supply. This vascular disruption causes segments of bone to become ischemic and necrotic, forming a **sequestrum**. In response, the living periosteum attempts to wall off the infection by laying down a shell of new bone, termed the **involucrum**. Openings may develop within this new shell, called **cloacae**, allowing purulent discharge to drain through sinus tracts to the skin surface. Understanding this triad of sequestrum, involucrum, and cloacae is vital for interpreting surgical findings and imaging reports.

headings.title: Classification and Etiology
headings.content:
Bone infections are broadly categorized by duration, route of acquisition, and underlying host status. 

- **Acute Osteomyelitis**: Characterized by symptoms lasting less than two weeks, common in children via hematogenous spread to long bone metaphyses.
- **Chronic Osteomyelitis**: Defined by persistence beyond several weeks or months, marked by dead bone pieces and recurrent flare-ups.
- **Hematogenous Osteomyelitis**: Results from bacteria seeding through the bloodstream from a distant focus such as a skin boil or respiratory tract infection.
- **Contagious Osteomyelitis**: Arises from direct inoculation via penetrating trauma, open fractures, or contiguous spread from infected diabetic foot ulcers.

Staphylococcus aureus remains the leading causative pathogen across all age groups and classifications. Other notable agents include Pseudomonas aeruginosa in puncture wounds through sneakers and Salmonella species in individuals with sickle cell disease.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment
headings.content:
Clinical presentation varies widely depending on whether the infection is acute or chronic, as well as the patient's age and immune status. 

- **Local Signs**: Constant, throbbing bone pain that intensifies with movement or weight-bearing, localized swelling, erythema, and localized warmth over the affected site.
- **Systemic Signs**: High spiking fevers, chills, general malaise, and irritability, particularly prominent in acute hematogenous cases.
- **Chronic Indicators**: Persistent or intermittent draining sinus tracts, non-healing cutaneous ulcers, and persistent low-grade pain without dramatic systemic spikes.

During assessment, examine the affected limb for guarding, restricted range of joint motion, and signs of neurovascular compromise distal to the lesion. Palpate carefully to identify focal point tenderness.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Findings
headings.content:
Confirming infective bone disease requires correlating clinical findings with laboratory assays and imaging modalities. 

| Investigation Type | Expected Finding / Utility | Clinical Timing |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Full Blood Count** | Elevated white blood cell count with a left shift | Initial screening |
| **Inflammatory Markers** | Elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate and C-Reactive Protein | Tracking treatment response |
| **Plain Radiographs** | Soft tissue swelling initially; bone destruction appears late (10-14 days) | Baseline imaging |
| **Magnetic Resonance Imaging** | High sensitivity for early bone marrow edema and inflammation | Early diagnosis |
| **Bone Biopsy & Culture** | Isolates the specific pathogen and determines antibiotic sensitivities | Definitive diagnostic standard |

Relying solely on early plain X-rays is a frequent clinical pitfall, as radiographic evidence of bone destruction lags significantly behind symptom onset.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Successful medical management centers on prolonged, targeted antimicrobial therapy tailored to culture and sensitivity results. Empiricist intravenous antibiotic coverage is initiated immediately after obtaining diagnostic blood and bone cultures, targeting Staphylococcus aureus and other likely local pathogens. Therapy typically extends over a prolonged duration—often four to six weeks or longer—to ensure eradication of bacteria sequestered within poorly vascularized bone matrix. Transitioning from intravenous to oral agents may occur once clinical improvement is noted and inflammatory markers decline, provided the chosen oral drug has high bioavailability and bone penetration. Supportive care includes adequate hydration, nutritional optimization to support wound healing, and appropriate analgesia.

headings.title: Surgical Interventions and Wound Care
headings.content: Surgical intervention becomes necessary when medical therapy alone fails, when an abscess or sequestrum is present, or when joint stability is threatened. Procedures include **debridement**, where all devitalized bone and infected soft tissue are aggressively excised to a bleeding, healthy bone margin (termed saucerization). **Decompression** involves drilling into the cortex to relieve high intraosseous pressure. In cases with significant bone defects, surgeons may utilize bone grafting or antibiotic-impregnated polymethylmethacrylate beads to deliver local concentrations of antimicrobials while filling dead space. Postoperative wound care requires sterile aseptic technique, management of surgical drains, and monitoring for signs of persistent infection or flap compromise.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care focuses on pain management, infection control, nutritional support, and preparing the patient for long-term recovery at home. Nurses monitor vital signs for systemic sepsis, assess wound dressings for purulent drainage or strike-through, and administer prescribed intravenous analgesics and antibiotics on schedule. Patient and family education must emphasize adherence to prolonged outpatient antibiotic regimens, recognizing signs of recurrence such as returning fever or localized swelling, and maintaining a high-protein, vitamin-rich diet to promote tissue regeneration. For patients discharged with peripherally inserted central catheters (PICC lines) for home IV therapy, teaching safe line maintenance and flush techniques is essential to prevent secondary line infections.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Prognosis
headings.content: Despite advances in antimicrobial therapy and surgical techniques, infective bone disease can lead to severe local and systemic complications. Chronic osteomyelitis frequently results in pathological fractures due to extensive cortical destruction and weakened bone integrity. Other long-term sequelae include limb-length discrepancies in growing children, joint contractures, secondary amyloidosis from prolonged chronic inflammation, and squamous cell carcinoma developing within long-standing draining sinus tracts (known as Marjolin ulcer). In severe or neglected cases, uncontrolled infection can progress to septicemia, multi-organ dysfunction, or necessitate limb amputation to save the patient's life.
